title: What If the Soviets Won the Moon Race? A New Show Spies on Their Secret Space City!
summary:
Imagine a world where the Soviet Union beat America to the moon. That's the story of the hit show "For All Mankind." But until now, we only saw the American side—NASA engineers scrambling to catch up. A brand-new spinoff called "Star City" finally pulls back the curtain on the other team.

"Star City" is named after a real training center near Moscow where Soviet cosmonauts (that's what they called astronauts) lived and practiced. The show is like a Cold War spy thriller, filled with brave space pilots, clever engineers, and sneaky KGB agents. They all work together—and sometimes against each other—to keep their country ahead in the race to the stars.

In real history, the Soviets actually beat the U.S. at many space firsts. Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961. Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space in 1963. But in the show's alternate timeline, the Soviets also plant their flag on the moon first. The new series follows a fictional cosmonaut named Anastasia Belikova, who becomes the first woman to walk on the lunar surface. Her path is full of secrets and struggles.

The creators say people often forget how successful the Soviet program was. "They were just knocking it out of the park," said co-creator Matt Wolpert. "Star City" lets us peek behind the Iron Curtain and imagine what might have been. It premiered May 29 on Apple TV.
why_it_matters: By exploring a 'what if' in history, you can see how science and exploration often rely on competition between nations, and how different the world might look if one small event changed.

background_read: In real history, the Space Race was a fierce competition between the United States and the Soviet Union (a group of countries once led by Russia).

The Soviet Union achieved many stunning firsts: Yuri Gagarin (a brave pilot) became the first human in space in 1961, and Valentina Tereshkova (a factory worker turned cosmonaut) became the first woman in space in 1963.

The new show 'Star City' takes place in a make-believe world where the Soviets also beat the U.S. to the moon, and it is named after the real training base outside Moscow where cosmonauts still train today.
Article_Structure: WHO: The show follows Soviet cosmonauts like fictional hero Anastasia Belikova, KGB agents, and the real historical figures who raced for space glory.
WHAT: A brand-new spinoff called 'Star City' imagines the secretive Soviet space program in a world where they planted the first flag on the moon.
WHERE: The story is set at the real Star City training center near Moscow and on the lunar surface itself.
WHY: The creators wanted to lift the Iron Curtain and show how successful—and dramatic—the Soviet side of the space race would have been if they had won.

perspectives.description: The show celebrates the bravery and smarts of Soviet scientists and cosmonauts who accomplished amazing things but are often left out of American space stories.
Some people worry that the show might make the Soviet Union look too good, forgetting that it was a country where the KGB spied on its own people and limited freedom.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral – alternate history as a mirror
perspectives.description: Using a made-up timeline lets viewers see both real history and their own world from a new angle, asking what happens when different teams play by different rules.
